new_entities.name: Delayed school start times
new_entities.description: Policies that shift school start time later in the morning for adolescents.

new_entities.name: Adolescent sleep duration
new_entities.description: Total sleep duration among adolescents, especially on school nights.

edges.effect_quant: A 2017 meta-analysis aggregating five longitudinal and 15 cross-sectional studies found later school start times were associated with longer student sleep duration, and a 2016 systematic review of experimental evidence reported weeknight sleep increases ranging from 25 to 77 minutes after start times were delayed by 25 to 60 minutes.
edges.population: middle-school and high-school adolescents exposed to later morning school start times
edges.mechanism: Later start times better align school schedules with delayed adolescent circadian timing, reducing forced early wake times and extending achievable weeknight sleep.
edges.summary: Delayed school start time is one of the strongest policy-level sleep interventions for adolescents. The evidence is consistent enough to treat it as a genuine protective factor for adolescent sleep duration rather than a speculative education-policy idea.
edges.caveats: The magnitude of benefit varies by baseline start time, commuting patterns, and student behavior. Not all downstream academic or mental-health outcomes improve equally, but the sleep-duration effect is among the most reproducible findings.

evidence.citation: Bowers JM et al 2017 Sleep Health
evidence.notes: Effects of school start time on students' sleep duration, daytime sleepiness, and attendance: a meta-analysis.

evidence.citation: Minges KE et al 2016 Sleep Med Rev
evidence.notes: Delayed school start times and adolescent sleep: A systematic review of the experimental evidence.

evidence.citation: Paksarian D et al 2015 Am J Public Health
evidence.notes: School Start Time and Adolescent Sleep Patterns: Results From the U.S. National Comorbidity Survey--Adolescent Supplement.
